items.title: The triangular bed
items.student: Illustrative school-garden plan, not a surveyed site. Triangle ABC has AB=10 m, AC=8 m and included angle BAC=30°. Sketch it and label the perpendicular height from C to AB. Can its area be 40 m²? Explain what information a gardener needs before buying cover material.
items.teacher: Height=8 sin 30°=4 m; area=1/2×10×4=20 m².40 m² wrongly treats AC as a perpendicular height. The plan is a mathematical model, not a claim about an actual school.

items.title: Build the triangle-area rule
items.student: Draw a triangle with a horizontal base b, adjacent side a, and an acute included angle θ. Drop a perpendicular height h from the far end of side a. Write sinθ in terms of h and a, then substitute into A=bh/2. Practice: a=12 cm, b=7 cm,θ=60°.
items.teacher: sinθ=h/a, so h=a sinθ and A=ab sinθ/2. Practice 21√3≈36.37 cm². The angle must be between the two named sides. Use degree mode. The derivation assumes the drawn acute configuration; it is sufficient for these tasks.

items.title: Three sides, no measured angle
items.student: Triangle with sides 13 m, 14 m, 15 m. Use Heron’s formula A=√[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)], where s=(a+b+c)/2. First verify the sides can form a triangle. Find s and A. Compare with a triangle with sides 3 m, 4 m, 8 m.
items.teacher: For 13, 14, 15: triangle inequalities hold; s=21 m; A=√(21×8×7×6)=84 m².3+4<8, so the second set cannot form a triangle and no area is calculated. Heron is supplied here; no proof required.

items.title: A scale plan and a measurement limit
items.student: A triangular plot has measured side lengths 65 m, 70 m, 75 m. A drawing uses 1 cm to 5 m. Find the drawn side lengths and the plot area using Heron. Explain why the numeric result is a model estimate if the field measurements were rounded.
items.teacher: Drawing 13, 14, 15 cm. Full plot s=105 m; A=2100 m². Linear scale 5 gives area scale 25, agreeing with 84×25. Measurement precision limits real accuracy; avoid claiming exact surveyed area.

items.title: Quadrilaterals from triangles
items.student: Sketch and label:(a) parallelogram base 12 m and perpendicular height 5 m;(b) trapezium parallel sides 8 m and 14 m, perpendicular height 4 m. Decompose into triangles or rectangle plus triangles. Find each area and explain why a sloping side cannot replace perpendicular height.
items.teacher: (a)60 m²;(b)(8+14)/2×4=44 m². Derive the formula from decomposition or two congruent copies. State which sides are parallel and where height is measured.

items.title: Diagonals and a general quadrilateral
items.student: (a) A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 8 cm. They meet at right angles and bisect one another. Find its area by four triangles.(b) A kite has perpendicular diagonals 12 cm and 7 cm; find area.(c) A general quadrilateral is split by a 10 m diagonal; perpendicular heights of the other two vertices to its line are 3 m and 4 m on opposite sides. Find total area.
items.teacher: (a)40 cm²;(b)42 cm²;(c)1/2×10×3+1/2×10×4=35 m². The diagonal-product rule requires perpendicular diagonals; it does not apply automatically to every quadrilateral. In(c), add the two nonoverlapping triangles.

items.title: Regular polygons and their centre
items.student: For a regular n-sided polygon of side s and apothem r (perpendicular from centre to a side), draw n congruent triangles. Derive A=nsr/2. A regular hexagon has side 4 cm and apothem 2√3 cm. Find its area.
items.teacher: Each triangle area sr/2; total nsr/2. Hexagon area 24√3≈41.57 cm². The apothem is not the circumradius. Equal-side lengths alone do not establish regularity; equal angles are required too.

items.title: The regular heptagon and octagon
items.student: Two regular polygons each have side 4 m:(a) heptagon, n=7;(b) octagon, n=8. Split a centre triangle into two right triangles to show r=(s/2)/tan(180°/n). Calculate the apothem and area, keeping intermediate digits. Give areas to 1 decimal place.
items.teacher: Heptagon r≈4.153043 m, A≈58.142599 m²→58.1 m². Octagon r≈4.828427 m, A≈77.254834 m²→77.3 m². Calculator in degrees; centre half-angle is 180°/n. It is acceptable to provide printed apothems if calculators cannot evaluate these angles; learners still derive area from triangles.

items.title: An irregular L-shaped bed
items.student: An L-shaped region is an outer 10 m by 8 m rectangle with a 4 m by 3 m rectangular corner removed. Draw its boundary and split it into two nonoverlapping rectangles. Find the area by two methods. Then explain why adding all outer side lengths would answer a different question.
items.teacher: Area 80−12=68 m². One valid decomposition is 10×5+6×3=68 m². Mark dimensions so the removed 4×3 rectangle is clear. Perimeter is boundary length, not area.

items.title: An irregular polygon from a plan
items.student: Plot the ordered vertices(0, 0),(8, 0),(8, 3),(5, 3),(5, 6),(0, 6) on squared paper, 1 unit=1 m. Join in order and return to(0, 0). Find area by decomposition, then by a bounding rectangle minus a missing corner. Explain the units.
items.teacher: One decomposition 8×3+5×3=39 m². Bounding rectangle 8×6 minus 3×3=39 m². Drawing should be L-shaped with a 3-by 3 upper-right corner missing. No shoelace formula is needed.

items.title: Choose and defend a covering estimate
items.student: A fictional garden contains separate, nonoverlapping beds C1 and C9. Find total area. Cover material costs KES 150 per m²; for this exercise buy exactly the area needed, with no waste, tax or delivery. Find cost. State two reasons a real order might differ.
items.teacher: 20+68=88 m²; cost {{C11cost:.0f}} KES. Real orders can differ due to cutting waste, measurement errors, packaging sizes, overlap or delivery. These are discussion limits, not permission to invent a percentage allowance. Do not add a triangle twice to a region already counted.

items.title: Independent assessment diagrams and data
items.student: All dimensions are illustrative. Draw and label each before solving. A: triangle two sides 6 m and 8 m with included angle 30°. B: triangle sides 5 m, 5 m, 6 m. C: trapezium parallel sides 6 m and 10 m, height 3 m. D: regular heptagon side 2 m, apothem 2.076521 m; regular octagon side 2 m, apothem 2.414214 m. E: rectangle 9 m×7 m with a 3 m×2 m corner removed.
items.teacher: Use Final Explanation for questions and teacher key for solutions. Areas: A12 m²; B12 m²; C24 m²; heptagon≈14.5 m²; octagon≈19.3 m²; E57 m². Printed apothems are rounded, so final answers are specified to 1 decimal place for D.
